questions.question: In digital IC design, why is an asynchronous reset signal standardly asserted asynchronously but de-asserted synchronously (known as 'asynchronous assert, synchronous de-assert') using a two-flip-flop reset synchronizer?
options: To prevent metastability and functional glitches caused by the reset release violating flip-flop recovery and removal timing checks
To eliminate the need for a dedicated low-skew reset distribution network across the chip
To ensure that all combinational logic outputs settle to a high-impedance (tri-state) condition during system power-up
To allow the reset signal to propagate faster than the system clock across long interconnect lines
To reduce dynamic switching power by clock-gating sequential registers prior to system reset

questions.question: According to the Method of Logical Effort used for sizing transistors in digital CMOS logic networks, what condition achieves the absolute minimum total propagation delay through an N-stage combinational path driving a fixed output load?
options: The electrical effort (effective fanout) must be progressively doubled at each successive stage along the path
Each stage along the path must be sized to bear an identical stage effort (fi = gi * hi)
The logical effort of the initial input gate must equal the parasitic delay of the final output driver
The transistor width ratio (P/N ratio) of every stage along the path must approach exactly 1.0
The parasitic delay of all stages combined must sum to zero by eliminating interconnect capacitance

questions.question: In microprocessor memory hierarchies, what is the fundamental functional distinction between a 'write-through' cache and a 'write-back' cache?
options: A write-through cache allocates a cache line only on a write miss, whereas a write-back cache allocates only on a read miss
A write-through cache requires tracking dirty bits per cache line, whereas a write-back cache tracks only valid bits
A write-through cache immediately updates lower-level memory on every store operation, whereas a write-back cache defers updates until a dirty line is evicted
A write-through cache cannot be used in multi-core systems, whereas a write-back cache operates exclusively with snooping protocols
A write-through cache performs stores asynchronously via a write buffer, whereas a write-back cache stalls the pipeline on every store

questions.question: Under the Total Store Order (TSO) memory consistency model (implemented by x86 processors), which specific memory access reordering is explicitly allowed by the hardware, potentially leading to outcomes that violate strict Sequential Consistency (SC)?
options: A Load operation being reordered before an earlier Load to a different memory address (Load-Load reordering)
A Store operation being reordered before an earlier Store to a different memory address (Store-Store reordering)
A Store operation being reordered after a later Store to the same memory address (Store-Store collapsing)
A Load operation being reordered before an earlier Store to a different memory address (Store-Load reordering)
Atomic read-modify-write operations being speculatively reordered ahead of prior uncommitted memory Loads

questions.question: In a multi-level microprocessor cache hierarchy, what is the primary operational consequence of enforcing a strictly inclusive policy in the shared Last-Level Cache (LLC) relative to the private upper-level caches (L1 and L2)?
options: The total usable storage capacity of the multi-level hierarchy is strictly maximized because data is never duplicated across levels
Private L1 and L2 caches are strictly prohibited from implementing write-back policies and must operate as write-through
Read hits occurring in private L1 caches must simultaneously broadcast an access update to the LLC directory
Coherence requests from other cores can bypass the LLC and interrogate private L1/L2 tags directly without filter lookup
Evicting or invalidating a line in the LLC requires the hardware to issue back-invalidation probes to purge that line from any L1/L2 cache holding it
